newsitem.title: USA: Mice used to create drugs for humans in U.S.
newsitem.headline: Mice used to create drugs for humans in U.S.

text.p: U.S. drug development company, Abgenix Inc., said on Sunday it had found a way to genetically alter mice with human DNA so they are capable of secreting antibodies to treat a range of human illnesses.
Scientists involved in the research said their findings were a breakthrough after decades of work to extend the function of the human immune system.

"We see the mouse as a very powerful factory to produce fully human antibodies with high affinity and specificity," the author of the study, Dr. Aya Jakobovits, told Reuters. Her study is published in the February issue of "Nature Genetics".
Abgenix, a unit of Fremont, California-based Cell Genesys Inc., has already used this technology to develop compounds it believes can combat different kinds of cancers and severe inflammation.
It said it planned to begin the first phase of clinical trials of the inflammation compound in the fourth quarter of this year.

A key part of the immune system, antibodies are proteins that work to weaken or destroy foreign toxins in the body. In their natural state, however, antibodies will not attack other human proteins, even when they are responsible for disease.

But when the human genes that produce antibodies are transferred into a mouse, and the mouse is then given a human disease-causing protein, it will respond by generating an antibody to fight that substance in the same way the human body responds to foreign substances.

Researchers have long theorized about using mice to create human antibodies but in the past failed to transfer the appropriate genetic material into the mouse, or to create antibodies the human body would not reject.

The Abgenix researchers, however, were able to transfer about 80 percent of the human genes responsible for antibody production into the mouse. They also found that when they stripped the mouse of its own immune system, it generated fully-human antibodies.
They say the technology is promising because it offers the potential to develop substances that will work specifically against disease sites without affecting the rest of the body.
